title: Krishna consciousness
hookLine: the name everyone calls them isn't their name. it's a line from their song
carry: krishna consciousness: keep krishna in mind
tomorrow: can someone not born Hindu belong at the Krishna feast?

cards: Saffron cloth, a drum on a strap, small brass cymbals, and a song with only a few words in it, going round and round on a city sidewalk. Passersby have a name ready: the Hare Krishnas. Here's the odd part.
That isn't their name. It's a line from their song, turned into a nickname. Their real name is longer, and it hides a bigger puzzle about who Krishna is.

teach.b: Their own name is the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, ISKCON for short. And the reason sits in a story. On the battlefield of Kurukshetra, Arjuna drops his bow and won't fight.
Krishna, his charioteer, talks him through it for seventeen chapters: duty, the self that never dies, work without clinging.
Then, near the very end, he says: hear my most secret word.

In paraphrase: fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, offer to me, bow to me, and you will come to me. Let go of every other duty and take refuge in me alone. Arjuna picks up his bow; his confusion, he says, is gone.
For these devotees, that last word is the whole program: keep Krishna in mind, not only while singing, but while cooking, working, walking to the bus. Now the puzzle.
Many Vaishnavas, devotees of Vishnu, honor Krishna as Vishnu come to earth. This lineage, from the Bengal saint Chaitanya, turns that around.
After listing Vishnu's descents, the Bhagavata Purana says: these are portions, but Krishna is the Lord himself.

So for them, Krishna is the source, Vishnu included. Other Hindus hold it differently: Advaita teachers speak of one reality beyond every form; devotees of Shiva or the Goddess place them at the center.
This lineage's answer is Krishna, and the nickname from the song sits on top of it.

how: Devotees in ISKCON temples chant the Hare Krishna mantra, study the Bhagavad Gita and try to offer their daily work, cooking and worship to Krishna.

o: a nickname, from their song, for a Krishna-centered lineage
a name for any group that sings Hindu songs in public
a rock band that toured with the Beatles in the sixties

games.q: what's inside the nickname — tap the pairs.
p: keeping Krishna in mind in every task

s: at the end of the Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna to fix his mind on him
he calls it his most secret word; devotees read it as their whole program.
for this lineage, Krishna is the Supreme Person, the source of all
Gaudiya Vaishnavas see Krishna not as one form among many, but as the source.
all Hindus understand Krishna the way the Hare Krishnas do
Hindus hold it differently; this is one lineage's clear answer.

games.q: your friend's mom keeps a small picture of Krishna by the stove and hums his name while she cooks. in ISKCON's terms, what's she doing?
o: keeping Krishna in mind through an ordinary task: Krishna consciousness.
decorating: a picture in the kitchen is mostly there for good luck.
nothing religious yet; devotion only really starts at the temple.
games.why: Krishna consciousness means keeping Krishna in mind in every task, the kitchen included. devotees read Gita 18.65 as the whole program.

practice: Devotees chant while they do ordinary things. Pick up something you'll use later today, a cup, a pen, your keys, and hold it.
Softly say the chant as you look at it: Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare; Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare.
If you don't pray, say quietly what you'd like to keep in mind while you use it, and notice how often the mind wanders off.

wordCard.voice: The Hare Krishnas: a nickname from a song, for ISKCON, a Krishna-centered lineage with roots in Bengal.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Krishna, the name at the center of this lineage's song and life.

carryVoice: Something to keep from Arjuna's chariot: Krishna consciousness, keeping Krishna in mind through every task. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.64–66 (my most secret word; fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, offer to me, bow to me, and you will come to me; take refuge in me alone)
Bhagavad Gita 1.47 and 18.73 (Arjuna sets down his bow; at the end he says his confusion is gone)
Bhagavata Purana 1.3.28 (after the list of descents: these are portions, but Krishna is the Lord himself)
